title: Paraeus: fallen faith is sick—habitual only, and does not justify until repentance
source_text: XIX. Quibus consentit Paraeus, in Bellarminum de Amissione Gratiae, lib. 1. cap. 7. Ubi docet fidelem in grave peccatum, ut David, prolapsum, amittere munditiem cordis, laetitiam salutis, solatium gratiae, bonitatem conscientiae, &c. Et postea docet in fideli qui hoc modo lapsus est, fidem justificandi actum non exercere. Fides, inquit, tunc dicitur justificare, quum actum proprium accipiendi remissionem peccatorum exercere potest, atque exercet. Hunc vero actum non exercet, neque exercere potest fides aegra, saucia, sordibus carnis oppressa, peccatorum compedibus quasi ligata. Et infra: Justificatis vero lapsis Deus non imputat peccata, nempe resipiscentibus; ante resipiscentiam certe imputat, infligendo poenas temporales, & imputaret etiam infligendo poenas aeternas, nisi resipiscerent. Ac tandem sic concludit, Tunc igitur fides in lapsis habitualiter tantum manens, proprie justificari dici, aut eos justificare, non potest.
pass_a_gloss: With whom Paraeus agrees, against Bellarmine on the Loss of Grace, book 1, chapter 7. Where he teaches that a believer who has fallen into grave sin, as David, loses cleanliness of heart, joy of salvation, consolation of grace, goodness of conscience, etc. And afterwards he teaches that in a believer who has so fallen, faith does not exercise the act of justifying. Faith, he says, is then said to justify when it can exercise, and does exercise, its proper act of receiving the remission of sins. But this act a sick, wounded faith, oppressed by the filth of the flesh, as if bound with the fetters of sins, neither exercises nor can exercise. And below: But to the justified who have fallen God does not impute sins—namely to those repenting; before repentance he certainly imputes, by inflicting temporal penalties, and he would also impute by inflicting eternal penalties unless they repented. And at length he thus concludes: Then therefore faith remaining in the fallen only habitually cannot properly be said to be justified, or to justify them.
pass_b_english: Paraeus: David-like falls cost heart-cleanness, joy, and conscience; justifying faith then lies sick.
Only habitual faith remains—and God still imputes until repentance restores the act of receiving pardon.
